item.title: Thoughts Are Like Viruses
item.description:
Theory of Mind

Thoughts Are Like Viruses

Resisting intrusive thoughts can make them more powerful.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Thoughts and viruses are inert and only active when they connect to live entities.
  • Unwanted thoughts link up physiologically because we fight them.
  • They become our identity, cognitive fusion; we can’t differentiate unwanted thoughts from physical threats.
  • Skills are required to separate you from your repetitive unwanted thoughts.

What is a virus? It is a small segment of genetic material, DNA or RNA, enclosed in a protein envelope. It is neither dead nor alive. It simply exists. Viruses are everywhere. For example, a tablespoon of fresh water contains up to 500 million viruses. The human body contains 100 trillion to one quadrillion of them, far surpassing the number of cells in your body (30 trillion). The vast majority interact with bacteria. They have no internal metabolism; they cannot attack; they just are. (1,2)

Each cell in your body has multiple receptors for various molecules that signal behaviors appropriate to the internal environment as it responds to the external environment. Viruses come in myriad shapes and dock with specific receptors on the cell membrane. The genetic material is injected, and it is game on. The virus is now active and can wreak havoc. The virus must dock with the cell to be functional.

Thoughts are also not alive. What are thoughts? They don’t even exist. They are patterns of electrical activity in the brain that become etched in with repetition. The synapses (the spaces between neurons) become more sensitive, and patterns become the path of least resistance.

Thoughts interpret your physiology

Physiology comes first. Every living organism interacts with its surroundings through physiological and motor responses to optimize survival. The essence of life is found in single-celled organisms, and complexity evolved. This has been true for billions of years. Homo sapiens evolved several hundred thousand years ago without complex language. Other Homo species were essentially as intelligent, but the unique rounded shape of the forehead allowed more complex function. Chimpanzees and bonobos are 98.8 percent genetically similar. Crude language originated about 100,000 to 200,000 years ago, and complex language with abstract thinking is between 50,000 and 70,000 years old. Humans can think about thinking, and the concept of time arose. Physiology's driving force is far more powerful than your conscious brain. (3,4,5)

Source: Uryadnikov Sergey/AdobeStock

Humans uniquely use complex language to interpret, conceptualize, and name these internal signals (emotions). Because our first biological imperative is to survive, much of our physiology is geared toward fight-or-flight. As a result, a disproportionate share of our thoughts is negative. We dislike these sensations and the unwanted thoughts that accompany them. However, the bigger problems stem from how we react to these negative thoughts. When we resist them, the body confirms they are threatening, further activating the threat response. This creates a loop of repetitive unpleasant thoughts that grows stronger with resistance. Why don’t we have trouble with repetitive positive thoughts? We don’t fight them. They drift in and out, creating a sense of safety. To embed them, you must train yourself to embrace them.

You are your thoughts

You may have heard the term “You are not your thoughts.” That statement is incorrect. Repetitive unpleasant thoughts are now fully integrated into your entire being, and fighting cannot and doesn’t help. It creates more entanglement, and you become your unwanted thoughts. One term for this phenomenon is cognitive fusion; these thoughts have now docked and have become powerful drivers of threat physiology.(6) It is a deadly downward spiral that is solved only by deeply understanding the problem and learning strategies to separate from your thoughts (defusion) and redirect your attention toward what you want instead of what you don’t want.

The COVID virus is an example. It is also inert until it docks with your body. It is a foreign invader that your body fights to eliminate. The entire immune system is activated, including small signaling molecules called cytokines. The damage comes from the assault on your body, driven by inflammatory cytokines. The virus is less the problem than the body’s response to it. The more intense the battle, the more damage is done.

Source: Pixelzone/AdobeStock

Consider unwanted thoughts. Like the COVID virus, they are inert. An infinite number of thoughts float in and out of our heads, with minimal effects. However, when we feel threatened, our reaction evolved into an incredibly intense alarm signal that humans label anxiety. Thoughts reflecting this physiological state are negative and often extremely unpleasant. With cognitive fusion, the brain cannot differentiate repetitive unpleasant thoughts from a real physical threat. In nature, one threat is dealt with at a time. For humans, unwanted thoughts never stop and worsen as fighting them confirms that they really are threats.

There are answers to repetitive unpleasant thoughts

The body’s response to viral invasion is to mount an immune response, which is normally effective. However, for a permanent foreign body, such as an organ transplant, or for an overactive immune response, there is only one answer: Suppress it. This is achieved with immunosuppressive medications. In other words, stop the reaction. With organ transplants, suppression is necessary long-term. When we remove suppression, an intense host-versus-graft reaction can be fatal. Does this sound similar to repressed unwanted thoughts?

Dealing with repetitive unpleasant thoughts is easier. The reaction is the problem, not the thoughts. The strategy is similar: you can train your body and brain to avoid reacting. Although deep healing occurs in a state of safety, you cannot achieve it while you are fighting thoughts. Two basic starting points for addressing this:

  • Defusing, separating from your thoughts
  • Learning strategies to calm the threat physiology.

Both are necessary.

Calm your body first

Calm Your Body, Heal Your Mind presents these principles in detail, focusing on developing skills to become a professional at living. That means facing life’s inevitable adversity head-on and learning to stimulate your brain to change in the direction you choose (neuroplasticity).

You can reduce repetitive unpleasant thoughts by learning to disengage from your thoughts and calm your reactions. Examples of disengagement include expressive writing, awareness, mindfulness, and cognitive behavioral techniques.

Calming the threat-response physiology is a multipronged approach of dynamic healing. Every living creature must process its circumstances (input), synthesize data from multiple inputs (your mind and body), and send signals (output) to create physiology and actions appropriate to the situation. Strategies can change the input, calm the body and nervous system, making it less reactive, and directly calm the threat response.

Neither viruses nor thoughts can harm you unless they connect to living cells. With viruses, we have no choice but to fight them with an immune response. But with thoughts, we have a choice. “Give up.”

“What do you mean, give up?”

Give up fighting the unwinnable battle against your unwanted thoughts and focus on creating the life you want. Healing comes from forward-moving action.

item.title: 5 Missing Rubrics From College Core Competencies
item.description:
Education

5 Missing Rubrics From College Core Competencies

What attributes do college students need to succeed?

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Standard rubrics have limitations for evaluating success in college students.
  • Fostering the mental health and well-being of students is an essential component.
  • A holistic perspective is needed to help students thrive in higher education and future careers.

With the Fall semester rapidly approaching, it’s time for college students to say goodbye to summer and return to campus life. This may entail a combination of anticipation and dread as balancing the pressures of academic success and personal well-being loom large. Studies show that academic stress has a profound impact on the emotional well-being of college students (Barbayannis et al., 2022). Consequently, positive emotions are associated with academic achievement and academic performance (Cao et al., 2024). Research also points to a steady increase in pressure from perfectionism and a fear of failure (Sohn, 2024). Since learning pressure often leads to learning burnout (Gong et al., 2023), it’s important to take a closer look at how college students are being evaluated.

Most colleges and universities use structured rubrics to assess specific components of course expectations in various assignments. In my years as a college instructor, this served as a mechanism for grading and providing formative and summative feedback to enhance learning. Rubrics are designed to help students better understand the course expectations, learning objectives, and track their progress throughout the semester. Although these guidelines aim to improve clarity and structure and decrease anxiety, this is not necessarily the case. Similar to other assessments, rubrics have advantages and limitations that should be taken into account (Ling, 2024).

Students are constantly being critiqued and judged on their level comprehension, organization, critical thinking, and proficiency, but which components for achievement are we neglecting? From a mental health standpoint, more emphasis should be placed on recognizing the following:

Resilience – Psychological resilience is a mitigating factor between learning stress and learning burnout (Gong et al., 2023). Among the most significant factors for psychological resilience are self-esteem, a sense of belonging, subjective well-being, and pro-environmental behavior (Song et al., 2024). College students with low resilience have limited coping and problem-solving skills to deal with life challenges and academic demands. Therefore, with greater awareness of the impact of resilience, educators and students can implement appropriate strategies for goal-setting, confidence-building, and stress-management.

Purpose – Studies indicate that a sense of mattering is linked to lower rates of depression and anxiety in college students (Sohn, 2024). Mattering and well-being go hand-in-hand, and this is fostered through having a distinct purpose. Adolescents who feel valued and significant to themselves and others possess a positive self-concept and are more capable of flourishing (Paradisi et all., 2024). Students with a strong sense of purpose, particularly, altruistic purpose, have more motivation and commitment to their education (Sharma & Yukhymenko-Lescroart, 2018). Purpose also enables students to distinguish self-worth from achievement, so they don’t define themselves by successes or failures. Parents, teachers, and mentors are instrumental in reinforcing this, by demonstrating acceptance, caring, and compassion regardless of grades.

Identity – A sense of purpose is also connected to the development of a student’s identity. Formation of identity requires self-acceptance and adopting a positive self-image, including strengths and weaknesses (Lee et al., 2025). Outside interests should be cultivated, so students are not overwhelmed with a singular focus on academics. Extracurricular activities are readily available in the college environment and promote social engagement. Students can also seek out volunteer opportunities to connect with the community in a meaningful way. Having students appreciate their unique qualities as individuals is another invaluable tool. A well-rounded identity enhances emotional intelligence, self-esteem, and self-reflection for ongoing development.

Authenticity – Authenticity in adolescence assists with healthy psychological development and the ability to thrive (Alchin, 2023). Therefore, possessing authenticity is a key element for well-being and attaining successful performance outcomes. Research demonstrates that parents who promote increasing independence in adolescents are also facilitating their authenticity (Alchin, 2023). By the time they reach college age, their level of independence and self-awareness should be more robust. Students who commit to being themselves without self-judgement are also more likely to reach their full potential. Self-acceptance is often a work in progress, but it lays the foundation for defining ones’ purpose and the ability to connect with others.

Passion – Without passion, there is no joy in learning. Students can get caught up in plowing through their coursework without any real interest in the content. A passion for studying is associated with greater well-being and mental health (Larionow & Gabrys, 2024). Thus, academic enjoyment is tied to self-regulated learning and positive psychological well-being (Sverdlik et al., 2021). While not every student will be self-motivated in this respect, a thirst for knowledge can be nurtured. An inspiring teacher can make all the difference, even if the subject matter isn’t compelling. Additionally, choosing a major that coincides with the students’ personality and career aspirations is optimal. This can be the impetus for becoming a lifelong learner and pursuing ongoing fulfillment.

College students celebrating graduation.
Source: Leon Wu/Unsplash

The college experience is a journey of exploration and discovery for intellectual and personal growth. Standard rubrics are necessary to ascertain a student’s knowledge, progress, and areas of deficiency that need to be addressed. Nonetheless, the mental health and well-being of students is of equal weight and consideration. A holistic rubric should encompass a wide range of criteria that illustrate the full picture. Considering the mounting pressure of academic expectations, the college community should serve as a welcoming, supportive resource for students. The preparation for a successful future entails a high degree of self-development, just as much as earning a professional degree in higher education.

item.title: What Is Scromiting and Why Is It Increasing So Dramatically?
item.description:
Cannabis

What Is Scromiting and Why Is It Increasing So Dramatically?

The cannabis-induced condition is now so common it has its own ER code.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Scromiting is a condition affecting cannabis users that combines intense vomiting with actual screaming.
  • An ICD-10-CM diagnosis code for this condition was introduced 10/2025, facilitating recognition and tracking.
  • During the 8 months from October 2025 through May 2026, ER visits for Scromiting jumped a remarkable 370%.
  • A new CDC report indicates that symptoms can potentially occur as early as the 1st year of cannabis use.
Source: chuck herrera from Pixabay

Over the last two decades, common inquiries around the procurement of cannabis have evolved from, “Will this get me high?” to “Will I ‘green out’ if I take more than one of these gummies?” Now, there’s a new and different cause for cannabis-related concern: “Scromiting.”

Scromiting is the name for a relatively recent condition affecting cannabis users, a portmanteau for the intense vomiting combined with actual screaming that defines it. While this may sound like something from an ancient scared-straight film like Reefer Madness or perhaps a contemporary horror flick, these disturbing, often frightening symptoms are the result of cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (CHS), a literally gut-wrenching disorder that triggers severe nausea and debilitating abdominal pain—with vomiting/retching occurring up to 4-5 times an hour, according to the Cleveland Clinic.[1]

People afflicted with CHS are presenting in hospital emergency rooms with increasing frequency. While ER cases doubled between 2017 and 2021, affecting around 2.75 million people in the US,[2] from January 2023 through September 2025, a recently published U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) report found that the rate of ER visits involving CHS remained largely steady. However, during the 8 months from October 2025 through May 2026, it jumped a remarkable 370%.[3]

What accounts for such a dramatic escalation? While the prevalence of CHS is likely accelerating, its sudden increase also directly correlates with the introduction of a specific ICD-10-CM (International Classification of Diseases) diagnosis code for CHS in October 2025—making the condition easier for doctors to identify and track. The impact of this change was immediate. In one month alone, from September to October 2025, CHS-involved ER visits jumped from 3.35 per 10,000 to 11.26 per 10,000. By May 2026, they had risen further to 13.10 per 10,000.[4]

Historically, there had been some controversy as to whether CHS was an actual condition. The ICD-10 code provided needed clarification and significantly increased awareness of the disorder, whose recurring nausea and uncontrollable vomiting may have frequently been misdiagnosed as another gastrointestinal issue.

Previously, the syndrome was thought to affect only heavy cannabis users, notably those who used on a daily basis over the course of years. But, according to the CDC report, emerging evidence suggests symptoms can occur much sooner than previously estimated; potentially even within the first year of cannabis use. Moreover, younger people—especially those ages 15 to 24, and females—accounted for a disproportionate share of CHS-involved ER visits.

For those who suffer from CHS, “scromiting” episodes can manifest within 24 hours of cannabis use. Medical complications from repeated recurrences can include erosion of tooth enamel, acute kidney injury, electrolyte imbalances, dehydration, weight loss, and even seizures, as well as kidney failure.

The form of cannabis consumed may impact how quickly symptoms appear. Vaping or “dabbing” (the inhalation of highly concentrated THC-based oils evaporated under high heat) appears to increase the risk of CHS. The CDC findings come as vaping usage increases, with at least 15 million teens now using electronic cigarettes. A study published in Cannabis and Cannabinoid Research found that those who used electronic vape cartridges developed chronic vomiting much faster than through smoking or edibles.[5]

The escalating potency of cannabis products may also be a factor. Since the 1990s, the average psychoactive content in marijuana has nearly quadrupled from roughly 4% to about 16% tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), according to data from the U.S. National Institutes of Health.[6] The skyrocketing potency is particularly relevant given the unique way THC is metabolized. Unlike alcohol and most other drugs—including cocaine, heroin, and other opioids—which are cleared from the body in 3-4 days, THC is stored in fatty tissues and released gradually over at least 30 days. As a result, those using potent cannabis regularly have higher levels of THC in their bodies. This represents a form of prolonged and more problematic THC exposure. Additional potential contributing factors include adolescents starting cannabis use at younger ages, along with generally reduced public concern about possible risks since its now legal and easily available in so many states.

The CDC’s findings shine a bright light on the risks, prevalence, and serious health effects of cannabis hyperemesis syndrome/scromiting, especially for young people. As the adverse consequences of expanding cannabis use become more clear, severe, and prevalent, the need to strengthen awareness and education efforts and resources becomes an increasingly essential public health priority.

item.title: The Science of Making Music Therapeutic
item.description:
Therapy

The Science of Making Music Therapeutic

We know music can change how we feel — but what makes it therapy?

Posted August 24, 2026

Most of us have experienced music affecting how we feel. Whether it be an energizing song before a big interview, or a lullaby that settled us as a child, music has the power to change our emotional state. These effects are real and meaningful, but they don't automatically constitute therapy.

During the past 25 years, Music Therapy has been researched and used in clinical practice. While it is sometimes misunderstood as simply playing pleasant or familiar music for someone who is sick, it involves a trained professional using music intentionally toward an individualized therapeutic goal. A licensed music therapist considers the patient's medical or developmental needs, observes how that patient responds, selects specific musical elements and interventions, and continually adapts the experience toward defined therapeutic goals.

In other words, the question is not simply, "What music would this patient enjoy?" It is, "What does this patient need, and how might music support that goal?"

The Patient Comes Before the Music

While you might hop into your car and make a decision on what playlist to choose based on your mood, a music therapist takes a much more strategic approach. They do not begin by asking "What music should I play?" But, rather, they answer a set of important questions about the patient, such as:

  • What is happening physiologically?
  • What is their developmental capacity?
  • Are they alert, distressed, fatigued, or overstimulated?
  • What is the therapeutic goal?
  • How are they responding as the intervention unfolds?
  • What role might the family or caregiver play?

One of the clearest examples comes from the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), where even seemingly gentle stimulation has to be considered extremely carefully.

Premature and medically fragile infants do not experience sound in the same way that healthy adults do. Their neurological and sensory systems are still developing, and their ability to tolerate stimulation varies according to developmental stage and medical condition. Throughout an intervention, the therapist continues monitoring signs that the infant is comfortable and appropriately stimulated while addressing the above questions.

As with most things in life, ongoing observation is at the core of this work. The patient's response determines what happens next.

More Music Is Not Always Better

The individualized approach of Music Therapy also challenges a common assumption that if music can be beneficial, more of it must be better. That is not necessarily true.

For premature infants, in particular, too much sensory input can become stressful. Guidance recommends adapting music interventions according to developmental stage. Very premature infants may initially tolerate only soft vocal sounds, while older infants may gradually tolerate humming, lullabies, or limited instrumentation. Therapists continually monitor physiological and behavioral responses along the way.

Music is not universally calming, and the same intervention will not produce the same response in every person. A trained therapist must know when to introduce music and when to change or stop it.

Different Goals Require Different Interventions

Music Therapy does not refer to one standardized activity. In neonatal care, breathing entrainment may use musical elements with the goal of supporting physiological regulation. Infant-directed singing can facilitate caregiver-infant interaction. A parent's voice may become part of an intervention, while family-centered approaches can incorporate personally or culturally meaningful songs adapted for the infant's needs.

Researchers have also begun examining these approaches through defined clinical outcomes. A 2013 study published in Pediatrics, for example, evaluated Music Therapy in premature infants in relation to vital signs, feeding, and sleep. Other studies have explored family-centered Music Therapy involving premature infants and their caregivers.

The evidence base continues to develop, and findings from one patient population cannot automatically be applied to another. But research gives clinicians a way to ask more specific questions about which interventions may help, for whom, and toward which goals.

What Makes It Music Therapy?

Music can comfort, connect, and bring joy all on its own. Music Therapy takes that power and applies it with clinical purpose. What makes it therapy is not simply the music being played, but the trained professional assessing why it is being used, observing how the patient responds, and adapting the intervention in real time to support a specific therapeutic goal.

item.title: Small Needle, Big Questions: GLP-1s in Your Golden Years?
item.description:
Aging

Small Needle, Big Questions: GLP-1s in Your Golden Years?

Losing weight fast at 65 is not the same as losing weight fast at 35.

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • For decades, the prescription was always the same: Eat less, move more. Then prepare for the guilt.
  • GLP-1 drugs, originally built for diabetes, are now being studied for a long list of other health benefits.
  • If seniors follow guidelines their doctors recommend, these new drugs can do remarkable things.
Source: Annushkka Ahuja / Pexels

Somewhere between the AARP card and knee consultations, a lot of us picked up a few pounds we never asked for. Men began cinching their belts lower to accommodate a midsection. Women saw their own waistlines and thighs take on new dimensions, not to mention feeling "matronly" in clothes they once thought looked sharp.

Aging is indeed both a privilege and a study in body-morphing. For decades, the prescription was always the same: Eat less, move more. Then? Proceed to feel guilty about both. These days there's a new option in the mix, one that comes in a pen, hypodermic, or pill instead of a lecture, and it's changing how doctors think about weight, metabolism, and possibly aging itself.

GLP-1 receptor agonists, sold under names like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound, mimic a gut hormone that tells your brain you've had enough and slows digestion so you actually feel full. In generic form, they're known as semaglutide and tirzepatide, but by any other name, they perform the same seeming miracles, especially if you've tried everything from Weight Watchers to Jenny Craig to Optavia to keto to intermittent fasting to sheer willpower and found yourself stuck.

These peptides, originally built for diabetes, were found to melt away pounds along the way, and are now being studied for a surprisingly long list of things that have nothing to do with belt size.

GLP-1 Drugs and Older Adults

A 2025 meta-analysis of 11 randomized trials, covering more than 85,000 people, more than half of them 65 or older, found GLP-1 drugs cut major cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death, and kidney complications in older adults. A 2026 study in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society went further, looking specifically at adults 80 and up with type 2 diabetes. It found GLP-1 therapy was linked to fewer major cardiorenal events and lower all-cause mortality compared with an older diabetes drug class, a population usually left out of trials because researchers assume it's too fragile to study. Apparently not.

There's also early research suggesting these drugs reduce inflammation and improve insulin signaling in ways that might help protect against cognitive decline. Also being explored is a possible link to lowering the risk of some obesity-related cancers. While both are worth watching, neither is yet proven. The word doing the heavy lifting in that research is "might," and it should stay there until bigger, longer studies say otherwise.

Some 2026 reviews go so far as to argue that GLP-1s touch nearly all 12 biological processes scientists associate with aging itself, from mitochondrial function to cellular cleanup systems.

What doesn't make it into social media ads is that losing weight fast at 65 is not the same as losing weight fast at 35. Up to 40 percent of the weight lost on these drugs can be lean mass rather than fat, and older adults already lose muscle faster than younger ones. Researchers call this anabolic resistance: Your muscles simply need more protein to hold onto themselves as you age. This is specifically a concern in older patients, and a 2026 review confirmed that measurable muscle loss shows up consistently in the data, even while long-term studies are being sorted out.

But wait. None of this is a reason to rule these drugs out. It's a reason to ask your doctor about protein intake and resistance training from day one. While seniors need to be especially cognizant of the risks, if they follow guidelines for diet and exercise, these new drugs can do remarkable things.

Balancing Benefits, Costs, and Side Effects

For a lot of older adults, especially those carrying real cardiovascular or metabolic risk, GLP-1s appear to offer benefits well beyond the number on the scale when under a doctor's supervision, with real attention paid to muscle and nutrition along the way. But OK. On to the cost, which can be significant if insurance doesn't cover them. And no. They’re not free from side effects. Nausea, the cost, and the muscle loss are conversations worth having up front with your physician. Don't believe everything you read online.

Personally speaking, my 42 lb. weight loss on GLP-1s has been nothing less than spectacular in my eyes, but it took me nearly a year and a half to get to my goal size and weight. There were months when I frustratingly lost ounces and not pounds, but I stayed the course. I am now off blood pressure meds and swimming laps three times a week to maintain muscle tone. And I swear I look better at age 74 than at age 60 merely because my silhouette finally syncs with my height. I sometimes don’t recognize myself in store windows as I pass by, as I had been overweight for 3+ decades.

Aging with grace isn't about white-knuckle denial or blind enthusiasm for the newest thing. It's about asking good questions, reading past the headline, and seeing what's out there for people our age. After all, if this new approach to healthy aging is all it’s cracking up to be, fighting waistline spread is only part of the equation. All I know is that the inflammation and risk all those extra pounds add take their toll on an aging body.
